Nike Alphafly 4 review

Carlos Sánchez on Nov 8, 2026 | Reviewed using methodology 2.3
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 0:00 Instaread
Sponsored by

Our verdict

94
Superb
  • Daily running45
  • Tempo84
  • Race96
  • Stability79

The Nike Alphafly 4 may no longer be Nike's flagship super shoe, but we still think it's a terrific racer. After putting it through our lab tests and runs, we believe it's the best Alphafly yet, with more bounce, less weight, improved traction and the most secure Atomknit fit we've experienced in the series. However, the ride remains noisy, the shoe still feels heavier than key rivals, and our outsole tests revealed disappointing durability. It's a clear step forward, but not the major redesign some runners were expecting after such a long wait.

Pros

  • Improved energy return
  • Softer ride compared with v3
  • Impressively stable for a max-stack super shoe
  • Amazing upper delivers impressive lockdown
  • The lightest Alphafly to date
  • Powerful, redesigned Air Zoom units
  • Increased shock absorption
  • Top-notch ventilation
  • Built to excel at marathons
  • Small price drop
  • Improved grip on dry and wet surfaces

Cons

  • Heavier than leading rivals
  • Outsole durability concerns
  • Less interesting for wide feet than the AF3
  • Still makes a lot of noise

Who should buy

Our testing makes it an easy pick for Alphafly 3 fans wanting an upgrade, marathoners after a stable, fast racer, runners who struggle with lockdown, and heavier, forceful runners.

Who should NOT buy

Poor abrasion results and a PEBA-based midsole make it a weak trainer; the PUMA Deviate Nitro Elite 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 suit intervals and tempo work better.

It is also heavy; we prefer the Nike Vaporfly 4 or ASICS Metaspeed Ray, or the pricier adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3.

Cushioning

Heel protection improves to 157 SA, but the forefoot reads 117 SA because the twin Air Zoom units and cutouts leave less foam. Heavier runners may want over 130 SA there.

Midsole softness

Note: Low measurement: softer. High measurement: firmer.

Both foams test soft (32.3 AC ZoomX LT, 30.0 AC ZoomX), clearly softer than version 3.

The lower layer is 57% softer; in the cold the foams firmed 17% and 4%, so ZoomX copes better.

Rocker

As with Nike's other super shoes, the forefoot rocker rises late and gently; the flared, bevelled heel barely changes.

Plate

The wide carbon Flyplate carries over to load the two Air Zoom units.

Its curve is also unchanged.

Air Zoom

The new pods (blue) are smaller, more fibrous and compress further than the orange Alphafly 3 units.

Still, the ride stays firm and mechanical rather than plush.

ZoomX LT

Under the microscope ZoomX LT looks elongated next to ZoomX's round beads. Nike claims up to 17% less weight and 8% more rebound, which our data supports.

Traction / Grip

Traction test

The Fast Shot rubber scored 0.58 on wet concrete, enough for a rainy race day.

That beats the Alphafly 3's 0.40, yet Nike still trails ASICS, adidas and PUMA on grip.

Outsole design

Most of the textured rubber sits under the forefoot, with two round pads beneath the Air Zoom units and new openings exposing foam.

The heel keeps two separate patches around a central cutout, now wider and shorter, that shows the plate.

Flexibility / Stiffness

Alphafly plates have always been very stiff, taxing the calves but rewarding strong runners.

Version 4 is 14.1% more flexible at 24.4N, yet still extremely stiff and possibly hard work for lighter runners.

Weight

Our men's US 9 weighed 6.7 oz (190g), 5.5% lighter than version 3 while keeping both pods and the full plate.

That is still well short of the lightest racers; Nike fans who want minimal weight can try the Streakfly 2 for shorter races.

Stability

Lateral stability test

A broad forefoot around the pods, midfoot cables in the upper and the wide plate keep this softer version steady.

Alphafly 3 fans who valued its stability will find it intact.
